screens.title: The Assembler: Design and Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we build the assembler — the first full software tool that runs on the Hack machine you constructed. The assembler translates human-readable Hack assembly into the exact 16-bit binary instructions the C P U accepts. This project matters because it ties together parsing, symbol management, and code generation: you will write a program that reads text, reasons about labels and variables, and emits correct machine words. We'll follow a clean, two-pass architecture: the first pass discovers labels and fills a symbol table, while the second pass resolves symbols and produces binary. Along the way you'll implement a Parser that classifies instructions, a Code module that maps mnemonics to binary fields, and a SymbolTable that stores predefined symbols, labels, and variables starting at address 16. A concrete example you will use is a short Add program that becomes six 16-bit lines of machine code. A common misconception is to think the assembler simply translates line-by-line; instead, many assembly programs contain forward label references that require the first-pass scan. By the end of the chapter you'll understand why the two-pass design is simpler, how variables are allocated, and how to structure your assembler in modules for clarity and reuse. Consider what it means to run code on a machine you built — that is the milestone this assembler achieves.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and verification. You will write an assembler that reads a. asm file, removes whitespace and comments, builds the symbol table in a first pass, and produces the. hack output in a second pass. You will test correctness using example programs such as Add, Max, Rect, and Pong, comparing your. hack files to the course references. screens.title: What the assembler does
screens.narratorSegment: An assembler is a translator that converts symbolic assembly language into machine-code instructions the C P U executes. In the Hack context the assembler reads Hack assembly files, recognizes A-instructions, C-instructions and labels, and writes 16-bit words where A-instructions begin with a 0 bit and C-instructions begin with 111. The assembler's responsibilities include parsing text, maintaining a symbol table that maps names to numeric addresses, and applying fixed translation tables for C-instruction fields. A concrete example is the small Add. asm program: each symbolic instruction like @2 or D=A becomes a specific 16-bit binary string. A frequent misconception is to treat assembly translation as simple string substitution; instead it requires address resolution because labels and variables stand for numbers that may be defined later. The assembler is the first program you write that runs on your own machine, so it validates your C P U and memory design. Key checks include: does @value produce the correct 15-bit address when value is numeric, and does a symbol resolve to the right R A M or ROM address? Reflect on this: when you run your assembler and the C P U executes the produced words, you are using software to test your own hardware design.

keyIdea.text: The assembler maps readable assembly into exact 16-bit machine words, handling parsing, symbol resolution, and code generation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › What the assembler does

Assembler responsibilities

Formal definition

Translate assembly text into 16-bit binary instructions, resolve symbols to addresses, and write one binary instruction per line to a .hack file.

Why it matters
  • Validates the CPU and instruction set you built.
  • Introduces parsing and code generation concepts used in compilers.
  • Teaches symbol management and memory allocation strategies.
Key Takeaway

An assembler is more than text replacement: it must resolve addresses, manage names, and generate bit-accurate output for the CPU to run.

Concrete example
@2
D=A
@3
D=D+A
@0
M=D
This assembly becomes these machine-code lines:
0000000000000010
1110110000010000
0000000000000011
1110000010000000
0000000000000000
1110001100001000
Misconception check: numeric @values map directly to addresses; symbols require lookup. If you replace every symbol by an immediate number you will produce incorrect code when labels are referenced before definition.

screens.title: Two-pass assembler architecture
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack assembler uses a two-pass architecture: the first pass finds labels and builds the symbol table; the second pass translates instructions to binary using that table. The first pass scans every non-empty, non-comment line and tracks ROM addresses for executable instructions. When it sees a label like (LOOP) it records LOOP → current ROM address. It also initializes predefined symbols such as R0–R15, SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT, SCREEN, and KBD. The second pass revisits each instruction, resolves symbols and numeric addresses, and emits 16-bit machine words. For variables, when the second pass encounters a symbol that is neither predefined nor a label, it assigns the next free R A M address starting at 16. A concrete example: if @i appears and i is new, assign i → 16, then emit 0000000000010000. A common question is whether a single-pass assembler is possible. It is, but it requires backpatching unresolved addresses or maintaining a list of forward references, which complicates the implementation. The two-pass design is simpler for an educational assembler and makes debugging straightforward: you can inspect the symbol table after the first pass and confirm label addresses before translation.

keyIdea.title: Two passes explained
keyIdea.text: First pass: collect labels and initialize predefined symbols. Second pass: translate instructions and allocate variable addresses starting at 16.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Two-pass architecture

Two-pass pipeline

1
First pass — symbol discovery
Scan lines, increment ROM address for instructions, and add labels to the symbol table with their ROM addresses. Initialize predefined symbols.
2
Second pass — translation
Resolve symbols and numeric addresses, allocate variables beginning at RAM address 16, translate A- and C-instructions to 16-bit binaries, and write the .hack file.
Variable allocation rule
When a new symbol appears in the second pass that is not predefined or a label, assign it the next free RAM address starting at 16, then use that address for the current and subsequent references.
Example walkthrough
Given lines: (LOOP) followed by three instructions. During the first pass, if the ROM address of the first instruction after the label is 4, we record LOOP → 4. Later, if we see @LOOP we replace it with 4 in the second pass and emit a binary A-instruction with 0 + the 15-bit binary of 4.
Misconception check
A single pass can work but requires storing unresolved references and patching addresses later. The two-pass approach avoids that complexity and is easier to reason about in an educational setting.
Why this process

The first pass guarantees all label addresses are known so the second pass can produce correct binary without deferred fixes.

screens.title: Symbol table: contents and lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: The symbol table is a dictionary mapping names to numeric addresses. It begins pre-populated with standard entries: R0 through R15 map to addresses 0–15; SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT map to 0–4 respectively; SCREEN maps to 16384 and KBD to 24576. During the first pass the assembler adds labels encountered as (LABEL) with their ROM address into the table. Labels represent locations in the instruction stream and therefore map to ROM addresses, not R A M. During the second pass, any symbol that is not predefined and not a recorded label is treated as a variable: the assembler assigns it the next free R A M address starting at 16. For example, the first time @i appears it will cause i → 16, the next new symbol @sum becomes 17, and so on. A common mistake is to allocate variables during the first pass; doing so can cause variable addresses to shift if labels or instruction counts are miscounted. Keep variable allocation strictly in the second pass so label addresses are stable before assigning R A M addresses. This lifecycle — predefined → labels → variables — keeps symbol resolution deterministic and easy to debug.

keyIdea.title: Symbol table lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Start with predefined symbols, add labels in the first pass with ROM addresses, and allocate variables in the second pass from RAM address 16 upward.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Symbol table

Symbol table contents

Predefined symbols
R0 → 0, R1 → 1, …, R15 → 15
SP → 0, LCL → 1, ARG → 2, THIS → 3, THAT → 4
SCREEN → 16384, KBD → 24576
Labels (first pass)
During pass one, when the assembler sees (LOOP) it sets LOOP → current ROM address. Example: (LOOP) at ROM address 4 adds LOOP → 4.
Variables (second pass)
When encountering @i where i is not in the table, assign i → next free RAM address starting at 16. Example: first @i → 16; first @sum → 17.
Misconception check: labels map to ROM addresses (instruction locations). Variables map to RAM addresses and should be allocated only in the second pass.
Practical tip

After the first pass, print the symbol table to confirm your labels and predefined symbols before running the translation pass.

screens.title: Translating A-instructions
screens.narratorSegment: A-instructions have the form @value. If value is a decimal number, the assembler converts it to a 15-bit binary string and prefixes it with a 0 bit to form the 16-bit instruction. If value is a symbol, the assembler looks it up in the symbol table and uses its address. If the symbol is not present and it's a variable, the second pass assigns a new R A M address starting from 16. A concrete example: @2 becomes 0 followed by the 15-bit binary of 2, producing 0000000000000010. If you see @i and i is a variable first used in the second pass, assign i → 16 and produce 0000000000010000. A common mistake is not zero-padding binary values to 15 bits; failing to pad or truncating will produce incorrect machine words. Below is a sample Python-style snippet that illustrates converting a numeric A-instruction into a 16-bit string. Use a verified conversion routine and test with small values and boundary values to be confident in your output. Translating A-instructions means numeric values become a 15-bit binary with a leading 0. symbols resolve to addresses in the symbol table; new variables get addresses starting at 16.. In practical terms, numbers vs symbols and how to emit 16-bit a-words. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Numeric values become a 15-bit binary with a leading 0. Symbols resolve to addresses in the symbol table; new variables get addresses starting at 16.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Translating A-instructions

A-instruction translation

Rules
  • If @value is numeric: convert to 15-bit binary, prefix with 0.
  • If @value is a symbol: look up in the symbol table and emit its address as binary.
  • If a new variable symbol appears in the second pass: allocate next RAM address starting at 16.
Common mistake: forgetting to left-pad the binary to 15 bits. Always format numbers to 15 bits before prefixing with 0.
Example conversion (conceptual)
# Conceptual Python-style pseudocode for conversion
value = 2
binary15 = format(value, '015b')  # yields '000000000000010'
instruction = '0' + binary15     # full 16-bit word
print(instruction)                # '0000000000000010'
Test with @0, @1, and a symbol @i. If i is new, during the second pass assign i → 16 and then emit 0000000000010000.

screens.title: Translating C-instructions
screens.narratorSegment: C-instructions have three conceptual fields: dest, comp, and jump. Their general form is dest=comp;jump, although dest or jump may be omitted. To translate a C-instruction, parse the text into its three parts, then use the Code module lookup tables to map comp, dest, and jump to their binary encodings. The final machine word is assembled as 111 + a + comp + dest + jump, where the initial 111 bits indicate a C-instruction. For example the instruction D=A is parsed as dest=D, comp=A, and no jump. Using the reference tables you compute the comp bits and dest bits and combine them into the 16-bit output. A common misunderstanding is to assume the textual order determines bit order; it doesn't. You must use the lookup tables to map each mnemonic into fixed-width bit fields and then concatenate them in the exact sequence required by the Hack specification. Practically, keep your Code module small and test each mapping entry; unit-test comp entries and short C-instructions so translation errors are easy to isolate. Translating C-instructions means parse dest, comp, and jump, then use lookup tables to map each mnemonic to fixed-bit fields and assemble the 111+a+comp+dest+jump word.. In practical terms, parsing dest=comp;jump into binary fields via lookup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: C-instruction mapping
keyIdea.text: Parse dest, comp, and jump, then use lookup tables to map each mnemonic to fixed-bit fields and assemble the 111+a+comp+dest+jump word.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Translating C-instructions

C-instruction parse & encode

Parsing rules
Split on '=' for dest and on ';' for jump. If '=' missing, dest is empty. If ';' missing, jump is empty. The remaining middle part is comp. Use the Code module to map each fragment to bits.
Assembly example
D=A
dest→D, comp→A, jump→(none). Lookup comp bits for A, dest bits for D, then assemble 111 + a + comp + dest + jump.
Combining bits
The output layout is fixed. Start with the 3-bit opcode 111, then the a bit, then the 6-bit comp field, the 3-bit dest, and the 3-bit jump. Test individual table entries frequently to ensure correctness.
Misconception check: comp, dest, and jump are not variable-length fields; the assembler must always produce the exact bit widths required by the Hack machine.
Pro tip

Separate parsing from code lookup: return a structured instruction (dest, comp, jump) and then translate with your Code module for easier testing.

screens.title: Assembler modules: Parser, Code, SymbolTable, Main
screens.narratorSegment: Organize the assembler into four modules for clarity and reuse. The Parser reads the input file, strips whitespace and comments, and classifies lines as A-instruction, C-instruction, or label while providing the parsed fields. The Code module contains translation tables for comp, dest, and jump; given a mnemonic it returns the appropriate bit string. The SymbolTable module implements a dictionary with add, contains, and get operations, and is responsible for storing predefined symbols, labels added in pass one, and variables allocated in pass two. The Main orchestrates the pipeline: it performs the first pass with the Parser to build the symbol table, then replays the Parser output in a second pass to emit binary instructions using Code and SymbolTable. A concrete benefit of this separation is testability: you can unit-test Code entries independently and dump Parser outputs to trace parsing errors. A common misconception is to mix responsibilities—embedding symbol management inside parsing or lookup logic makes the code harder to test and reason about. Keep modules narrow and well-defined to speed debugging and future reuse in compiler-like projects. In practical terms, a modular pipeline for clarity and testing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module responsibilities

Parser
Reads lines, strips comments/whitespace, and returns structured instruction objects: type, symbol/value, dest, comp, jump. Keep parsing deterministic to simplify the passes.
SymbolTable
Dictionary with methods: addEntry(symbol, address), contains(symbol), getAddress(symbol). Initialize with predefined symbols before pass one.
Code module
Lookup tables for comp, dest, and jump. Each lookup returns a fixed-width bit string used to construct the final C-instruction word.
Main
Runs pass one with Parser to fill SymbolTable with labels. Then runs pass two to translate each instruction using Code and SymbolTable and write the .hack file.
Practical layout
This separation helps you unit-test the Code module entries and print Parser outputs. If your binary output differs from reference, inspect the symbol table and parser output to isolate whether the bug is in parsing, symbol resolution, or code lookup.

High-level steps

screens.title: Example translation: Add.asm walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the canonical Add. asm example so you see the exact translation process. The assembly lines are @2, D=A, @3, D=D+A, @0, M=D. First, there are no labels here, so the first pass simply initializes predefined symbols and counts ROM addresses for each instruction. In the second pass, @2 is numeric: convert 2 to 15-bit binary and prefix with 0 to get the first machine word. D=A is a C-instruction: parse dest=D and comp=A, look up comp bits for A and dest bits for D, then assemble 111 + a + comp + dest + jump. Continue for @3 and the following C-instruction D=D+A. @0 becomes the 16-bit A-word for address 0, and M=D is translated as a C-instruction writing D into memory. After translation you will have six binary lines which should match the reference. hack file. A misconception to avoid is relying on manual mapping; instead, use the Code module for comp and dest mappings to avoid human error. After you run your assembler, compare the output exactly with the reference; identical lines confirm correct parsing, symbol handling, and code generation.

screens.title: Common pitfalls, testing, and platform limits
screens.narratorSegment: When building the assembler watch for a few recurring pitfalls. First, ensure you correctly remove comments and blank lines; otherwise your ROM address counting in the first pass will be off. Second, initialize all predefined symbols exactly as specified — a missing or wrong predefined entry like R7 or SCREEN will produce wrong addresses. Third, allocate variables only during the second pass to prevent address drift. For testing, use the supplied examples (Add, Max, Rect, Pong) and compare. hack outputs to the reference. If outputs differ, print the symbol table after the first pass and list parsed instructions before translating — this narrows the problem to either symbol resolution or code mapping. Regarding limits: variables are allocated starting at R A M address 16; the practical variable space before colliding with stack conventions is normally from 16 to 255, yielding about 240 variables in typical educational use. Remember this is a platform constraint to keep in mind when testing very large assembly programs. Final reflective question: can you spot an input that would force a single-pass assembler to backpatch addresses? Thinking about that clarifies why the two-pass approach is simpler to implement and debug.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Pitfalls & limits

Testing and common errors

Common mistakes
  • Counting comment lines as instructions during pass one.
  • Allocating variables in the first pass instead of the second.
  • Incorrect or missing predefined symbols in the initial table.
  • Not zero-padding numeric A-instruction binaries to 15 bits.
Testing approach
Run your assembler on the provided programs and compare your .hack output to the references. When mismatches occur, print the cleaned instruction list, the symbol table after the first pass, and the parsed instruction that led to the differing binary.
Platform note
Variables allocate from RAM address 16 upward. In typical use you can expect roughly 240 simple variable slots before colliding with conventional stack starting areas; plan tests accordingly if your assembler will be run on very large programs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas in mind as you implement the assembler. First, the two-pass design: pass one builds the symbol table by registering labels and initializing predefined symbols; pass two resolves symbols, allocates variables starting at 16, and emits binary. Second, the symbol table content and lifecycle: predefined symbols, labels assigned ROM addresses during the first pass, and variables assigned R A M addresses during the second pass. Third, the modular pipeline: Parser to classify and extract fields, Code to map mnemonics to bits, SymbolTable to manage names, and Main to orchestrate both passes. These three concepts make the assembler understandable, testable, and reliable. When you test with Add, Max, Rect, and Pong, use the symbol-table dump and a line-by-line binary comparison to find discrepancies. Ask yourself: does the symbol table after pass one reflect label addresses correctly? If yes, then translation errors are likely in the Code module or parsing.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we build the assembler — the first full software tool that runs on the Hack machine you constructed. The assembler translates human-readable Hack assembly into the exact 16-bit binary instructions the C P U accepts. This project matters because it ties together parsing, symbol management, and code generation: you will write a program that reads text, reasons about labels and variables, and emits correct machine words. We'll follow a clean, two-pass architecture: the first pass discovers labels and fills a symbol table, while the second pass resolves symbols and produces binary. Along the way you'll implement a Parser that classifies instructions, a Code module that maps mnemonics to binary fields, and a SymbolTable that stores predefined symbols, labels, and variables starting at address 16. A concrete example you will use is a short Add program that becomes six 16-bit lines of machine code. A common misconception is to think the assembler simply translates line-by-line; instead, many assembly programs contain forward label references that require the first-pass scan. By the end of the chapter you'll understand why the two-pass design is simpler, how variables are allocated, and how to structure your assembler in modules for clarity and reuse. Consider what it means to run code on a machine you built — that is the milestone this assembler achieves.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the two-pass assembler architecture, implement the Hack assembler, and manage the symbol table. Specifically, you will learn to perform a first pass to collect labels and predefined symbols, and a second pass that resolves symbols and produces correct 16-bit machine words. You will implement the assembler in a high-level language, applying parsing techniques, lookup tables for C-instruction fields, and a dictionary-based symbol table. A practical milestone is to generate. hack output that matches the course reference for programs such as Add and Max. Why this matters: writing the assembler is the first time you produce software that runs on the machine you built and introduces compilation concepts used by later modules. A common misconception is to treat variables like labels; variables are assigned R A M addresses starting at 16, while labels map to ROM addresses. Each objective helps you reason about code generation and debugging when your output deviates from the reference.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and verification. You will write an assembler that reads a. asm file, removes whitespace and comments, builds the symbol table in a first pass, and produces the. hack output in a second pass. You will test correctness using example programs such as Add, Max, Rect, and Pong, comparing your. hack files to the course references. Practical debugging skills include tracing the symbol table contents and checking translated instructions line by line. A typical concrete task is: run your assembler on Add. asm and verify the six binary lines match the reference exactly. A common pitfall is mis-allocating variable addresses or failing to initialize predefined symbols like R0–R15 and SCREEN; both cause incorrect translations. This objective stresses reproducible testing: if your output differs, inspect the parser output and the symbol table entries to find the mismatch. The ability to test and debug is as important as writing the translator itself.

An assembler is a translator that converts symbolic assembly language into machine-code instructions the C P U executes. In the Hack context the assembler reads Hack assembly files, recognizes A-instructions, C-instructions and labels, and writes 16-bit words where A-instructions begin with a 0 bit and C-instructions begin with 111. The assembler's responsibilities include parsing text, maintaining a symbol table that maps names to numeric addresses, and applying fixed translation tables for C-instruction fields. A concrete example is the small Add. asm program: each symbolic instruction like @2 or D=A becomes a specific 16-bit binary string. A frequent misconception is to treat assembly translation as simple string substitution; instead it requires address resolution because labels and variables stand for numbers that may be defined later. The assembler is the first program you write that runs on your own machine, so it validates your C P U and memory design. Key checks include: does @value produce the correct 15-bit address when value is numeric, and does a symbol resolve to the right R A M or ROM address? Reflect on this: when you run your assembler and the C P U executes the produced words, you are using software to test your own hardware design.

The Hack assembler uses a two-pass architecture: the first pass finds labels and builds the symbol table; the second pass translates instructions to binary using that table. The first pass scans every non-empty, non-comment line and tracks ROM addresses for executable instructions. When it sees a label like (LOOP) it records LOOP → current ROM address. It also initializes predefined symbols such as R0–R15, SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT, SCREEN, and KBD. The second pass revisits each instruction, resolves symbols and numeric addresses, and emits 16-bit machine words. For variables, when the second pass encounters a symbol that is neither predefined nor a label, it assigns the next free R A M address starting at 16. A concrete example: if @i appears and i is new, assign i → 16, then emit 0000000000010000. A common question is whether a single-pass assembler is possible. It is, but it requires backpatching unresolved addresses or maintaining a list of forward references, which complicates the implementation. The two-pass design is simpler for an educational assembler and makes debugging straightforward: you can inspect the symbol table after the first pass and confirm label addresses before translation.

The symbol table is a dictionary mapping names to numeric addresses. It begins pre-populated with standard entries: R0 through R15 map to addresses 0–15; SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT map to 0–4 respectively; SCREEN maps to 16384 and KBD to 24576. During the first pass the assembler adds labels encountered as (LABEL) with their ROM address into the table. Labels represent locations in the instruction stream and therefore map to ROM addresses, not R A M. During the second pass, any symbol that is not predefined and not a recorded label is treated as a variable: the assembler assigns it the next free R A M address starting at 16. For example, the first time @i appears it will cause i → 16, the next new symbol @sum becomes 17, and so on. A common mistake is to allocate variables during the first pass; doing so can cause variable addresses to shift if labels or instruction counts are miscounted. Keep variable allocation strictly in the second pass so label addresses are stable before assigning R A M addresses. This lifecycle — predefined → labels → variables — keeps symbol resolution deterministic and easy to debug.

A-instructions have the form @value. If value is a decimal number, the assembler converts it to a 15-bit binary string and prefixes it with a 0 bit to form the 16-bit instruction. If value is a symbol, the assembler looks it up in the symbol table and uses its address. If the symbol is not present and it's a variable, the second pass assigns a new R A M address starting from 16. A concrete example: @2 becomes 0 followed by the 15-bit binary of 2, producing 0000000000000010. If you see @i and i is a variable first used in the second pass, assign i → 16 and produce 0000000000010000. A common mistake is not zero-padding binary values to 15 bits; failing to pad or truncating will produce incorrect machine words. C-instructions have three conceptual fields: dest, comp, and jump. Their general form is dest=comp;jump, although dest or jump may be omitted. To translate a C-instruction, parse the text into its three parts, then use the Code module lookup tables to map comp, dest, and jump to their binary encodings. The final machine word is assembled as 111 + a + comp + dest + jump, where the initial 111 bits indicate a C-instruction. For example the instruction D=A is parsed as dest=D, comp=A, and no jump. Using the reference tables you compute the comp bits and dest bits and combine them into the 16-bit output. A common misunderstanding is to assume the textual order determines bit order; it doesn't. You must use the lookup tables to map each mnemonic into fixed-width bit fields and then concatenate them in the exact sequence required by the Hack specification.
